meta.blurb: Solomon Northup was a free Black man, a husband, a father and a fine violin player, living in New York. In 1841 two strangers tricked him, and he woke in chains. This is his true story of twelve years of bondage, and of the day he was found.
meta.bible: Solomon Northup: born free in Minerva, New York, in July 1808; a farmer, a carpenter and a Violin player; kidnapped in Washington in 1841 and held as a slave for twelve years; freed in January 1853; the author of the book, published in 1853. Mintus Northup: his father, born into slavery and freed on the death of his master; died in 1829. Anne Hampton: his wife, married on Christmas Day 1829. Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo: their three children. Brown and Hamilton: the two men who tricked him with a promise of work as a musician. James Burch: the slave dealer who held him in Washington. Eliza: a woman held with him, with her children Emily and Randall. Theophilus Freeman: the slave dealer of New Orleans, who called him Platt. William Ford: a Baptist preacher and kind master in the Pine Woods of Louisiana. John Tibeats: a cruel carpenter. Chapin: Ford's overseer, who saved him. Edwin Epps: a harsh cotton planter at Bayou Boeuf, Louisiana, who held him for about ten years. Mary Epps: his wife. Patsey: the best cotton picker on Epps's plantation. Armsby: a poor white labourer who betrayed him. Samuel Bass: a Canadian carpenter, an opponent of slavery, who wrote the letters that saved him. Henry B Northup: the New York lawyer, from the family that once owned Solomon's father, who came to find him. Washington Hunt: the governor of New York. Judge Turner: the judge at Marksville. David Wilson: the New York writer who helped him to write the book. William Henry Harrison: the President whose funeral Solomon saw in April 1841. Places: Minerva, Saratoga Springs, Sandy Hill, New York, Washington, the Capitol, Richmond, Virginia, New Orleans, Louisiana, Red River, Pine Woods, Bayou Boeuf, Marksville, Georgia, Canada. Key terms: Slavery, Overseer, Plantation, Cotton, Sugar cane, Violin, Mortgage, Abolition, Kidnapping, Brig, Steamboat, Swamp, Bayou, Hunt. Voice and tone: serious, dignified and clear; cruelty is stated plainly and briefly, never graphically; the writer respects Solomon Northup's courage and quotes nothing from his book at length.

A1A2: In 1853, Solomon Northup told the true story of his stolen life.
Solomon was born free in New York in 1808, in the month of July.
His father taught him to read, and Solomon learned to play the violin.
On Christmas Day in 1829, Solomon married a woman named Anne.
In 1834, the family moved to Saratoga Springs, where there were more jobs.
In March 1841, two men offered Solomon a job playing music.
In New York City, he got a paper that said he was free.
In Washington, Solomon saw a big funeral march through the streets.
That night, Solomon felt very ill after he had supper with the men.
When Solomon woke up, he was in a dark room, in chains.
A man named Burch told him he was a slave from Georgia.
In the pen, he met a woman called Eliza and her children.
At night, they were taken by boat and train to Richmond.
A big ship carried them from Richmond to New Orleans.
In New Orleans, a dealer called him Platt and put him up for sale.
Eliza was taken away from her children, and she cried for them.
A man named William Ford bought Solomon and took him to Louisiana.
Solomon was clever, and he found a better way to move timber.
Ford had money problems, so Solomon was given to a cruel man.
When Tibeats tried to beat him, Solomon fought back and won.
Tibeats came back with a rope, and tried to hang Solomon.
At last, Ford came and cut him down from the rope.
Later, Tibeats attacked him again, so Solomon ran into the swamp.
Ford helped him, but in the end Solomon was sold to Epps.
Edwin Epps was a hard man who often drank and used the whip.
Every day, they had to pick a set weight of cotton.
At night, they slept only a few hours on a hard plank.
A young woman called Patsey was the best cotton picker of all.
In the sugar season, Solomon cut cane and earned a little money.
He made ink and a pen, and secretly wrote a letter.
A man named Armsby promised to post it, but he told Epps.
The years went by, and Solomon missed his family very much.
In 1852, a carpenter named Samuel Bass came to work for Epps.
Bass told Epps plainly that slavery was wrong, and Epps laughed.
Solomon trusted Bass and told him his real name and story.
Bass wrote letters to Solomon's friends in New York State.
Solomon waited and waited, but no one came for him.
In January 1853, two men arrived at Epps's farm in a carriage.
In the field, a man said his real name, and Solomon looked up.
Epps was angry, but he could not stop them taking Solomon.
At Marksville, a judge agreed that Solomon was a free man.
He and Henry Northup travelled north by boat and by train.
Burch was brought to court, but the law did not help Solomon.
In January 1853, Solomon came home to his wife and children.
With help from a writer, Solomon wrote down his whole story.
Many people read the book, and it sold very well.
Solomon spoke at public meetings and told his story to crowds.
After 1857, nobody knows for sure what happened to Solomon.
Slavery in the United States ended in 1865, twelve years later.
Today, people all over the world still read his true story.
B1B2: In 1853, a book appeared in New York with the title Twelve Years a Slave. Its author, Solomon Northup, was a free man who had been stolen from his family and sold into slavery.
Solomon was born in July 1808 in Minerva, a small town in New York State. His father, Mintus, had once been a slave, but he was set free when his master died.
Mintus taught his son to read and write, which was unusual in those days. Solomon also learned to farm, and he loved to play the violin more than anything.
On Christmas Day 1829, Solomon married Anne Hampton, and they worked hard to build a home. They had three children, named Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo.
In 1834, the family moved to Saratoga Springs, a busy town with many hotels. Solomon found work in the hotels and on building sites, and Anne worked as a cook.
In March 1841, two well-dressed men met Solomon in the street. They said they were with a circus, and they offered him good money to play the violin for a few weeks.
The men took Solomon to New York City, where he got an official paper that proved he was a free man. Then they all travelled on to Washington, and he expected to be home in a few weeks.
They arrived in Washington in April 1841, on the day before the funeral of President Harrison. Solomon stood among the crowds and watched the great procession pass through the streets.
That evening, the men took Solomon to supper and offered him wine. He soon felt very ill, and he remembered almost nothing after that.
When Solomon woke, he was lying on a cold stone floor in the dark, with heavy chains on his hands and feet. His money and his free papers had disappeared completely.
A slave dealer named James Burch came to the cell and said that Solomon was a runaway from Georgia. Solomon said that he was a free man from New York, but Burch beat him until he stopped.
In the slave pen, Solomon met a woman called Eliza, who had two children, Emily and Randall. They were also going to be sold, and Eliza could not stop crying.
One night, Burch had them taken out of the pen in secret. They travelled by boat and by train to Richmond, in Virginia, where they were put in another slave pen.
A ship called the Orleans carried them from Richmond to New Orleans. During the voyage, a disease called smallpox spread among them, and a man named Robert died of it.
In New Orleans, a slave dealer named Theophilus Freeman took charge of the captives. He gave Solomon a new name, Platt, and made him ready to be sold.
Eliza was sold away from her children, and she begged to be kept with them. Solomon never forgot the sound of her crying, and he wrote about it for the rest of his life.
A man named William Ford bought Solomon and took him up the Red River to Louisiana. Ford was a Baptist preacher, and Solomon thought that he was a kind man.
Solomon worked at Ford's sawmill, and he thought of a way to float the timber down the creek on rafts. Ford was pleased with his clever idea, and he praised Solomon.
Ford had money problems, and he handed Solomon over to a carpenter named John Tibeats. Tibeats was cruel and quick to anger, and he found fault with everything that Solomon did.
One day, Tibeats tried to whip Solomon over a small mistake with some nails. Solomon had never been so angry, and he took the whip from his hand and beat him with it.
Tibeats came back with two other men and a rope, and they tried to hang Solomon from a tree. Chapin, Ford's overseer, arrived with pistols and stopped them before it was too late.
Late in the afternoon, Ford came back and cut the rope. Solomon was alive, but he had suffered terribly in the heat and he knew how close he had come to death.
Tibeats attacked him again, this time with an axe. Solomon took it away and ran, and he spent a night and a day in the swamp before he reached Ford's house.
Ford kept him safe and hired him out to another farmer for a time. In about 1843, Solomon was sold to a planter named Edwin Epps, who lived on Bayou Boeuf.
Edwin Epps was a hard man who drank too much and used the whip often. He believed that the people he owned were his property, and that he could do anything he liked with them.
Every day, each worker had to pick a certain weight of cotton, and it was weighed at night. Anyone who fell short was whipped, so Solomon had to learn to pick quickly.
At night, they went back to a bare cabin and ground their own corn for supper. They slept for a few hours on a plank, and then they had to be in the fields again at dawn.
Patsey was a young woman who could pick more cotton than anyone on the plantation. Epps treated her cruelly, and his wife Mary was jealous and unkind to her.
At harvest time, Solomon learned to cut sugar cane with a long knife. Other planters hired him for the season, and he was able to keep a little of the money.
Solomon wanted to write to his friends in New York, but he had no ink, no pen and no paper. He made ink from tree bark, a pen from a duck's feather, and took a sheet of paper.
A poor white worker named Armsby promised to post the letter for money, but he told Epps instead. Solomon told Epps a clever lie, and then he burned the letter.
The years went by, and Solomon kept thinking about his wife and children. He knew that they were growing up without him, and he wondered whether they had given up hope.
In 1852, a carpenter from Canada named Samuel Bass came to build part of Epps's house. Solomon worked beside him, and he soon saw that Bass was different from other white men.
Bass told Epps to his face that slavery was wrong, and that all people should be free. Epps laughed at him, but Solomon listened carefully, and his hope grew.
One night, Solomon decided to trust Bass, and he told him the truth. He said that his name was Solomon Northup, and that he was a free man from New York.
Bass wrote letters to Solomon's friends in Saratoga Springs and told them where he was. He sent them carefully, and he knew that the answer would take many weeks to come.
Solomon waited through the autumn, and Christmas came and went. Bass went home to Canada, and still no one came, and Solomon began to lose hope.
In January 1853, a carriage arrived at Epps's farm with a lawyer named Henry Northup and a sheriff. They had official papers signed by the governor of New York.
Solomon was working in the field when the lawyer asked him some questions about his past. When he said the name Solomon Northup out loud, Solomon recognised his old friend at last.
Epps was very angry, but the papers were official, and he could not stop them from taking Solomon. As he rode away, Patsey ran after him, crying, and he felt great sorrow.
In the town of Marksville, Judge Turner listened to the evidence and agreed that Solomon was a free man. The legal papers were completed, and he was free to go.
Solomon and Henry Northup began the long journey north by steamboat and by train. In Washington, they went looking for the people who had sold him.
Burch was arrested for kidnapping, but at that time a Black man could not speak against a white man in court there. Burch went free, and Brown and Hamilton were never brought to justice.
In January 1853, Solomon came home to New York, where his wife Anne and his children were waiting. The children were grown up now, and there was a baby grandson named after him.
Solomon wanted people to know the truth, so he agreed to write a book. A writer named David Wilson helped him, and the book was published later in 1853.
The book was a great success, and it sold many thousands of copies in its first years. People who read it asked hard questions about slavery, and its true story shocked them.
After the book came out, Solomon spoke at public meetings in the northern states. He told his story in person, and crowds came to hear him.
Very little is known about the end of Solomon's life. He was last mentioned in about 1857, and historians have never found any record of when or where he died.
Solomon never forgot the people he left behind, such as Patsey, whose fate is not known. Slavery in the United States ended in 1865, twelve years after he was freed.
Today, people around the world still read Solomon Northup's story. It is one of the clearest and most truthful accounts of slavery, and it reminds us that freedom belongs to everyone.
C1C2: In 1853 a book appeared in New York whose title said exactly what had happened to its author, and the whole country began to talk about it. Solomon Northup had been born free, yet he was kidnapped in 1841 and forced to live as a slave in Louisiana for twelve years. A local writer named David Wilson helped him to put the story on paper, and Northup swore that every word of it was true.

Solomon Northup was born in July 1808 in the small town of Minerva, in the hills of New York State, and he was free from the first day of his life. His father, Mintus, had once been a slave in a family that bore the same name, but when his master died he was set free by the terms of the will. Solomon was proud of that fact, and he recalled his father as an honest, respected man who worked hard and never left his family hungry.

Mintus believed in education, and he taught his son to read, write and work with figures, which few free Black farmers could afford to do in those years. Solomon grew up working the land beside his father, but what he loved most was the violin, and he played it so well that people came from miles around to hear him. He later wrote that it was a gift that brought him pleasure, though it also played a part in the trap that was set for him.

On Christmas Day in 1829, the year in which his father died, Solomon married Anne Hampton, a young woman of mixed African, European and Native American descent. They farmed a small piece of land, worked for neighbours when they could, and soon had three children, whom they named Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo. Solomon later described those years as simple and happy, and he said that he had never once imagined that they could end so cruelly.

In 1834 the Northups moved to the town of Saratoga Springs, where rich visitors filled the hotels in summer and where a willing man could find plenty of work. Solomon took jobs in the hotels, on building sites and on the railroad, and he played his violin at parties, while Anne gained a fine reputation as a cook. They were never wealthy, but they were respected, their children were going to school, and he believed that his life had settled into a good and steady pattern.

In March 1841, when Solomon was thirty-two, two well-dressed strangers who called themselves Brown and Hamilton approached him in the street and praised his skill with the violin. They said that they belonged to a travelling circus, that they were waiting for it in Washington, and that they would pay him generously to play for a few weeks. Solomon was short of money and eager to accept, and since Anne was away working as a cook in another town, he decided that the offer was worth a short trip.

The two men led Solomon first to New York City, and he took the sensible precaution of going to an office to obtain an official paper which proved that he was a free citizen. They then travelled on towards Washington, and Solomon fully expected to be back at home within a few weeks, with a pocketful of money for his wife and children. He left no word for Anne, because there seemed no reason to do so, and it was a decision that he would regret for years.

The travellers reached Washington in April 1841, just as the nation was mourning the death of its President, William Henry Harrison, who had died only a few weeks into his term. Solomon stood among the crowds that lined the streets and watched the great funeral procession pass, never suspecting that the capital of the land of freedom would soon be the scene of his own disaster. The two men kept him close, and they spoke kindly to him throughout the day.

That evening the two men took Solomon to supper and pressed several glasses of wine upon him, and afterwards he began to feel sick, then dizzy, and then very ill. He remembered being helped to a bed and seeing a doctor, but after that his memory dissolved into a fog, and he later believed that he had been given a drug in his wine. The last thing he could recall was a sense of sinking, as if the floor of the world had given way beneath him.

When Solomon came to his senses, he found himself sitting on a cold stone floor in near darkness, with heavy chains locked around his wrists and ankles. His pockets were empty, his money and his precious free papers had vanished, and the two friendly men who had brought him to Washington were nowhere to be found. For a long time he could not understand what had happened, and he thought that there must have been some terrible mistake.

A slave dealer named James Burch soon appeared in the cell and told Solomon that he was a runaway slave who had come from Georgia, which was completely untrue. When Solomon insisted that he was a free man from New York, the dealer and his helper beat him until he could hardly move, and they told him that he must never again speak of being free. From the small yard of the slave pen he could see the dome of the Capitol, which only made his captivity more bitter.

In the slave pen Solomon met Eliza, a woman who had been separated from the people she knew, and who had with her a young son named Randall and a small daughter named Emily. They were all to be sold, and although Eliza had once been promised her freedom, no one now cared about that promise, and she wept for her children day and night. Solomon felt sorry for her, though he could do nothing, as he had suddenly become a prisoner himself.

One night Burch had the prisoners chained together and taken out of the pen in secret, put on a steamboat and then on a train bound for Richmond in Virginia. There they were locked in another pen, where more captives were waiting, and Solomon tried to find a way of sending news to his friends, without success. Every mile took him farther from the world he knew, and every hour made it harder to believe that anyone would find him.

The prisoners were put aboard a brig called the Orleans, which sailed from Richmond towards the port of New Orleans, and Solomon later wrote that it was a terrible voyage in cramped and dirty conditions. Smallpox broke out among them, and one of the captives, a man named Robert, became ill and died, while Solomon himself fell sick but recovered. After a stormy passage the ship finally reached the mouth of the Mississippi and moved slowly up the river to the city.

In New Orleans the captives were handed over to a slave dealer named Theophilus Freeman, who had them washed, dressed in new clothes and drilled so that they would appear cheerful to the buyers. Freeman gave Solomon a false name, Platt, and gave him the false story that he had been born a slave, and Solomon was beaten whenever he protested. It was as if his true name and his real life had been quietly erased by the stroke of a pen.

The dealer sold Eliza apart from her children, and in spite of her tears and her desperate pleading she was parted from them for ever. Solomon never forgot the sight of her grief, and in his book he wrote of it with deep feeling, so that readers might understand that slavery tore apart the closest bonds of family. He recalled that the dealer scolded her for weeping, as though a mother's sorrow was no more than a nuisance to be controlled.

Solomon was bought by William Ford, a Baptist preacher who owned land in a district of Louisiana known as the Pine Woods, on the Red River. Ford treated the people he held with more kindness than most masters, and Solomon wrote that he seemed to be a gentle man who was blinded to the injustice of slavery only by custom and habit. Even so, Solomon was not free, and he never stopped thinking about the family that he had left behind in New York.

Ford had a sawmill, and he needed a quick way to move the timber to market across the creek and through the swamps. Solomon, who was practical and observant, proposed floating the logs down the narrow waterway on rafts, and the plan worked far better than anyone had expected. Ford was delighted by the saving in time and money, and he praised his new worker as an unusually intelligent man, a compliment that Solomon had to hide behind a careful silence.

Ford fell into debt, and in order to repay what he owed he sold Solomon to the carpenter John Tibeats, though he kept a mortgage on his property and promised to protect him. Tibeats was a small-minded and spiteful man who resented Solomon's skill, and he found fault with everything that he did, however carefully the work was done. Solomon, who had been treated with some decency by Ford, now felt the full weight of his powerlessness.

One morning Tibeats flew into a rage over the size of some nails and tried to whip Solomon, and for the first time in many months Solomon's anger overcame his fear. He seized the whip, wrestled the carpenter to the ground and gave him a thorough beating, which he did not regret, although he knew at once that the consequences might be deadly. Tibeats ran off to fetch help, vowing that he would see Solomon pay for it.

Tibeats returned with two companions and a rope, and they dragged Solomon beneath a tree and began to prepare a noose around his neck. At that moment Chapin, who was Ford's overseer, rode up with a pistol in each hand and ordered them to stop, declaring that Solomon belonged to Ford and was not theirs to harm. The danger was over, but Solomon was left tied with the rope on his neck for many hours, with his toes barely touching the ground.

It was late in the afternoon before Ford came riding home, and when he saw what had been done he cut Solomon down and spoke gently to him. Solomon was alive, though his neck was bruised and his wrists were swollen, and the long hours in the burning sun had left him numb with pain and exhaustion. He wrote later that the whole experience showed him how little his life weighed in the eyes of the law in that place.

Some time later Tibeats attacked him again, this time with an axe, but Solomon snatched it from him and ran for his life into the swamp. He waded through black water for a night and a day, among snakes, alligators and clouds of mosquitoes, until he finally came out near Ford's house, exhausted but alive. He later said that the swamp, with all its dangers, had seemed safer than the man who was hunting him.

Ford sheltered Solomon and, in order to keep him out of Tibeats's reach, hired him to another farmer for a season, where the work was hard but the treatment was fair. Eventually, however, Solomon was sold once more, and in about 1843 he became the property of a planter named Edwin Epps, whose farm lay beside a slow river called Bayou Boeuf. It was the start of a darker chapter, and he would remain with Epps for about ten years.

Edwin Epps was a rough, hard-drinking planter who farmed cotton on the Bayou Boeuf, and Solomon described him as a man who could be amusing one minute and savage the next. Epps used the whip freely, and he claimed that the Bible gave him the right to do so, as the people he held were his property to treat as he wished. Solomon learned to keep his head down, to say very little and to watch the moods of his master as a sailor watches the sky.

Every worker on the plantation had to pick a set weight of cotton from before dawn until after dark, and each evening the sacks were carried to a weighing house to be checked. Anyone whose sack was too light was whipped, and Solomon, who had never picked cotton before, struggled to learn the skill. Over time he grew faster, but he was always aware that his safety depended on a scale and the temper of Edwin Epps.

When the day's work was finally done, the workers returned to a bare cabin, where they had to grind their own corn and cook their meagre supper of cornmeal and bacon. They slept for only a few hours on a hard plank with a thin blanket, and when the horn sounded at dawn they were back in the fields. Through it all Solomon kept his violin, and its music remained the one thing in his life that still belonged to him.

Among those held by Epps was Patsey, a young woman who could pick far more cotton in a day than any man on the plantation and who had a lively, spirited nature. Epps treated her with cruelty, and his wife, Mary, who was jealous of the attention he paid her, made her life still harder. Solomon wrote that she was the most wronged person he ever knew, and that he could do almost nothing to protect her.

In the autumn the sugar harvest began, and Solomon, who handled the long cane knife as skilfully as anyone, was hired out to neighbouring planters. The work was exhausting, but the arrangement allowed him to earn a little money of his own at Christmas, and he often played his violin at parties, where he met a few kinder people. Year followed year in this way, and each Christmas he wondered whether he would ever return to Saratoga.

Solomon longed to send word to his friends in New York, but he had no ink, no pen and no paper, and writing a letter was a serious offence for a man in his position. He boiled the bark of a tree to make a dark ink, cut a pen from the feather of a duck, and carefully took a single sheet of paper from the master's desk. By the light of the fire he wrote a letter, and he hid it in his clothes, hoping for a chance to send it.

A poor white labourer named Armsby, who worked in the fields for a few weeks, agreed to carry the letter to the post office in return for money, and Solomon trusted him. Armsby, however, went straight to Epps and told him everything, hoping for a reward, and Solomon only escaped a severe punishment by inventing a story that made the man look like a liar. That night he burned the letter in the fire, and he learned never again to trust a stranger.

The seasons turned from planting to picking and back again, and Solomon counted the years in cotton harvests while his hope slowly faded. He thought constantly of Anne and of his children, who would be growing up without a father, and he wondered whether they still believed he was alive or whether they had long ago given him up for dead. He kept himself going by living day to day, because the thought of the years ahead was far too heavy to carry.

In the summer of 1852 a carpenter named Samuel Bass, who had been born in Canada, came to work on a new building at Epps's plantation, and Solomon was assigned to help him. The newcomer spoke frankly, treated Solomon as an equal and showed no fear of Epps, and Solomon began to suspect that here, at last, might be a man who could be trusted. For several weeks he watched Bass very carefully, hardly daring to hope that he was right.

One afternoon Bass and Epps fell into a heated argument, and the Canadian declared in front of everyone that slavery was a great wrong and that all people were equal in the sight of God. Epps merely laughed and called him a dreamer, but Solomon, who overheard it, felt a rush of hope that he had not known for years. Bass was a man who spoke his mind, even when it was dangerous, and that was exactly the kind of man that Solomon needed.

One night, Solomon took the greatest risk of his life and told Bass the truth: he was Solomon Northup, a free man from Saratoga Springs, kidnapped eleven years before. Bass listened in silence, deeply shocked, and then he promised that he would do everything he could to help, though he warned that they must be extremely careful. Solomon wrote that this was the moment when he first felt the weight of the chain begin to lift.

True to his word, Bass wrote to two of Solomon's old acquaintances in Saratoga Springs, Mr Parker and Mr Perry, and told them where the missing man was and under what name he was being kept. The letters were posted at once, but the distance was great, and Solomon understood that he would have to wait many weeks for any reply. He went back to the cotton fields with his secret, and he kept his face as still as stone.

Autumn came and the weeks crept by, and the carpenter finished his work and went north to Canada, promising that he would do all he could to bring help. Christmas came and went without a word from New York, and Solomon, listening for the sound of a carriage on the road, began to fear that his friends had never received the letters at all. Hope, he found, was both a comfort and a torment, because it made the waiting harder to bear.

In January 1853, a carriage rolled up to the Epps plantation carrying a sheriff and a lawyer named Henry Northup, who came from the same family that had once owned Solomon's father and who had known him in his youth. They had travelled all the way from New York, with official papers signed by Governor Washington Hunt, after Solomon's friends had received Bass's letter and begged the state to act. It was the result of months of effort by people who had never forgotten him.

Solomon was picking cotton in the field when the lawyer walked up and began to ask him a series of questions about his past, which he answered, at first, with his false name of Platt. Then Henry Northup called him by his real name, Solomon Northup, and the two men stared at one another, until all at once Solomon recognised his old friend from home. He later described this as the happiest moment of his whole life, and he said that he could hardly speak for joy.

Epps was furious when he learned the truth, and he stormed and threatened, but the papers were genuine and the sheriff was present, so there was nothing that he could do. Solomon had time for only a few words of farewell to the people he had lived beside for years, and as the carriage drove away, Patsey ran after it with tears streaming down her face. He wrote that it was one of the saddest moments of his life, because he could not take her, or any of them, with him.

In the nearby town of Marksville, the judge examined the papers and the statements of Solomon's friends and found that the proof of his identity was complete. Epps gave up his claim, and the legal formalities were finished in a few short hours, though it had taken twelve years to begin them. When he walked out of the courthouse, he felt lighter than he had in more than a decade.

The two men set out for the north by steamboat and railroad, travelling day and night through the cold of January, and Solomon, wrapped in a new coat, could hardly believe that he was truly free. When they reached Washington, Henry Northup was determined that the men who had stolen his friend should answer for what they had done, and they went at once to search for them. It was a strange and bitter experience for Solomon to return to the city where his troubles had begun.

Burch was arrested for kidnapping, but the law of the time did not let a Black man speak against a white man in a Washington court, so the case failed. The dealer left the court a free man, and the two men who had tricked Solomon with the promise of work were never brought to answer for their crime, which is a bitter fact of the story. Northup found it hard to accept that justice had failed him in the very shadow of the Capitol, yet he refused to stop telling the truth.

In January 1853 Solomon Northup returned to the town of Sandy Hill, New York, where his wife Anne and their children had been waiting for twelve long years. His son and daughters were almost grown, and his daughter Margaret introduced him to a baby boy who had been named Solomon Northup Staunton, after the grandfather he had never met. He wrote that the joy of that reunion could not be described, and that he would never forget the faces of the family that had been given back to him.

Solomon wanted the world to know what had been done to him and to others like him, and so he sat down with a writer named David Wilson, who helped him to shape his memories into a book. The work was finished in a matter of months, and the book was published later in 1853, with its full title proclaiming that its author was a citizen of New York who had been kidnapped in Washington City in 1841. Wilson said that he had tried to add nothing, and that the story had been written down exactly as he had heard it.

The book was an immediate success, selling many thousands of copies in its first few years and winning praise from newspapers across the northern states. Readers who had never thought much about slavery were suddenly confronted with a true story told by a man who had suffered it, and many of them were shocked into asking hard questions. The campaigners against slavery were delighted to have so powerful a witness on their side, and they quoted his account at their meetings.

After the book came out, Northup travelled around the northern states giving talks, and crowds came to hear him tell his story with his own voice and his own face. He spoke calmly and clearly, without anger, and audiences were deeply moved, because they understood that this was not a tale but a testimony. Some accounts say that he also helped people to escape from slavery, though the details have not survived.

Remarkably little is known about the later years of Solomon Northup, and historians have been unable to establish what became of him after about 1857. No record of his death has ever been found, and although several explanations have been offered, none of them can be proved. It is a strange and sad silence for a man whose voice had once been heard by thousands of readers across the world.

Solomon never forgot those he left behind in Louisiana, among them Patsey, and the book is a reminder that millions of others were never rescued by a letter or a lawyer. Slavery in the United States finally came to an end in 1865, after a terrible civil war, twelve years after Solomon himself had been set free. For the rest of his life he had to live with the memory of what had been done to him, and with the knowledge of how many others suffered the same fate.

More than a century and a half later, the true story of Solomon Northup is still read around the world, in dozens of languages, as one of the clearest first-hand accounts of slavery ever written. It reminds us that freedom is not a gift that one person may give or take from another, and that the courage of a single man, together with the kindness of a few others, can change a life. Solomon Northup came home, and by telling his story so plainly, he left the rest of us a duty to remember.
